cells: AFTER THE DIAGRAM / CALCULATION  |  Observe → (accuracy if needed) → aim + prediction → investigate surprises → choose next maths
Use this AFTER an actual figure or calculation, not from a predicted outcome. Short student-authored reflections; one clear observation and one reasoned next step often suffice.
Ask accuracy only if it is new, unresolved or consequential. Reuse documented measurement/precision limits from C24; avoid redundant explanations.
Unexpected findings are valuable: state what differs, consider a plausible alternative CHECK, and keep the original prediction visible. Never force a result to match.
Only suggest 1–3 contextual next actions on request, using the student's confirmed observed feature, type of IA, aim, actual data and course. Planned PMCC alone isn't evidence of linearity.
Examples are questions, NOT diagnoses or ready-made prose. Students may reject them, change the mathematics, or Save with an unresolved observation.
ID
Actual context / observation
Show only when student has confirmed
Ask: what do you ACTUALLY see?
Accuracy: only if NEW/unclear
Aim, original prediction and beneficiary
Plausible NEXT mathematical question
If unexpected or unclear, investigate
Do not imply / stage guardrail
Status
Statistics | scatter, roughly straight-line
Student confirms paired data and points appear approximately linear
What direction, spread and rough linear form do you ACTUALLY see? Are there clusters or unusual points?
Use previously confirmed input precision/coverage; ask again only for a NEW issue.
How does a possible linear association answer the aim? Is direction as predicted, and what might it mean for the intended beneficiary?

If the student reports roughly straight (not near-perfect) data and quantifying LINEAR association would help the aim, consider PMCC NEXT. If already clearly straight, ask whether PMCC adds any real value. A fitted line may matter more for prediction.
If a straight-ish pattern contradicts the prediction, acknowledge that, check variables/range, and state why quantifying the new pattern could help.
A scatter plot doesn't prove linearity, PMCC isn't yet performed, and association alone isn't causation.
Agreed
Statistics | scatter, visibly curved
Student confirms curved or changing-slope pattern from actual scatter, especially after predicted linear trend
Does the direction or steepness change? Where does the curvature appear?
Check whether the apparent bend exceeds known measurement variability; don't repeat C24 unprompted.
A curve may challenge the original linear expectation; does a different model better answer the aim?

If curved, consider whether monotonic or turning/cyclical; examine course-appropriate nonlinear modelling first. Spearman is an optional option only for suitable monotonic association, if in student's course/teacher-approved, not all curves.
Rather than forcing PMCC, ask whether the variable definitions, data range or different regimes explain the curve.
Don't claim a particular quadratic/exponential form solely from appearance.
Agreed
Statistics | scatter, weak or no apparent association
Student reports points look scattered or relationship unclear
Is there a consistent direction or merely an indistinct cloud? What are the observed limits?
If scatter/noise is substantial relative to expected effect, note uncertainty and sample scope only when not covered.
Does no obvious association challenge the prediction, and what decision can/can't this evidence support?

A genuinely absent/unclear trend may merit a cautious interpretation. PMCC is not required; if visual evidence is ambiguous, student may choose a justified quantitative check rather than forcing a positive result.
Explore a plausible narrower range/subgroup ONLY with a reason, or check variable definitions, rather than searching until a positive result appears.
A weak visual pattern isn't proof of no population association; don't invent one.
Agreed
Statistics | scatter with surprising extreme observation
Student actually notices one/few unusual plotted observations
What makes this point unusual in context? Could it be a genuine part of the data?
Review data entry/source precision ONLY when there is specific reason for concern.
How much does it change the story and prediction? Would ignoring it misrepresent the intended population?
Check the source value; later, when genuinely calculating correlation/model, assess sensitivity to this point.
Keep the genuine point unless a documented reason excludes it; an unexpected value might reveal something useful.
PMCC outlier sensitivity is a technique-specific limitation at C40/C50, not automatically at scatter construction.
Agreed
Statistics | single variable appears bell-shaped
Student reports a roughly symmetric, single-peaked histogram of numerical observations
How symmetric is the shape, and what spread or tail behaviour can you actually see?
Check whether bins/data resolution distort apparent smoothness, if a new issue.
Would a particular distribution model help with the probabilities or comparison in the aim?
If suitable for the course and actual data, explore a normal model and relevant descriptive measures later.
If the histogram differs from normal prediction, describe the difference first and compare appropriate alternatives.
Appearance is not proof of normality; don't automatically calculate model probabilities.
Agreed
Statistics | skewed, clumped or multimodal histogram
Student observes asymmetry, several peaks or marked grouping
What does the skew or clustering imply about typical values and variability?
Consider effect of data binning/source when genuinely material.
How does this affect any predicted normality and who might benefit from comparing subgroups?
Consider median/IQR, appropriate centre/spread measures or a justified group comparison.
Investigate whether groups/time periods could reasonably explain more than one cluster, rather than forcing a single normal curve.
Don't invent separate populations or causation from a histogram.
Agreed
Statistics | side-by-side comparison, visible group difference
Student reports meaningful difference in location/spread on common-scale plots
Which centre, spread or unusual values differ between groups?
Use real sample sizes and measurement resolution when judging strength of visible difference.
Does the difference support the prediction? What advice can be cautiously drawn for the stated group?
Calculate appropriate summary measures and, if course-appropriate/needed, later a suitable comparison method.
If direction differs from prediction, check group definitions, ranges and possible confounders before claiming the inverse.
Don't infer significance or causality from different-looking boxes/bars alone.
Agreed
Statistics | group plots unexpectedly similar
Student expected a group difference but common-scale plots show little
Are the groups alike in centre, spread, or both? Do the scales hide an actual small difference?
Consider group sizes and uncertainty before treating no visible difference as precise equality.
What would a lack of meaningful difference mean for the original advice/choice?
Compare relevant summaries; consider whether study can support a cautious null/inconclusive interpretation.
Check whether the intended contrast is the right variable and whether another meaningful comparison has a rationale.
Don't alter axes to manufacture a visually dramatic difference.
Agreed
Statistics | categorical bars/proportions
Student has counts/proportions across categories/groups
Which relative proportions appear different? Are the denominators comparable?
Small counts may make apparent percentage changes unstable; don't repeat earlier coverage checks.
Which category pattern directly bears on the aim and expected usefulness?
Compute defensible conditional proportions or later a suitable course test when really used.
If proportions conflict with prediction, inspect group definitions/denominators and sampling rather than ignoring result.
No long raw tables; don't force chi-squared unless categories and question warrant it.
Agreed
Statistics/modelling | time series looks periodic
Student observes repeated ups/downs over actual ordered measurements
How many visible cycles, and are intervals/peaks broadly consistent?
Is time sampling dense/precise enough to see the cycles? Ask only when material.
Would a recurring pattern help the original aim or predicted future behaviour?
If evidence supports it, investigate period/amplitude or a sinusoidal model within course scope.
If cycles are less regular than predicted, compare a simpler trend or note limited evidence.
A single rise-and-fall needn't establish true periodicity.
Agreed
Statistics/modelling | expected cycle absent
Student predicted periodicity but actual series appears irregular or mainly trending
What trend or variability replaces the expected repeating pattern?
Check observation span or sampling frequency if this might conceal a cycle.
How does the result revise the original decision or prediction?
Consider a trend/rate analysis, or explicitly investigate whether more cycles would be needed.
Re-examine period assumptions and time interval before constructing a decorative sinusoidal model.
Don't extend time range or fabricate extra data to show a cycle.
Agreed
Modelling | expected exponential vs observed changes
Student predicted percentage growth but observed interval differences/ratios vary
Are absolute differences or percentage changes roughly stable over meaningful equal intervals?
Check rounding and variable units if differences are small.
Which model would produce predictions relevant to the aim and beneficiary?
Compare evidence for linear versus exponential forms as substantive next mathematics.
If growth seems closer to constant difference than constant percentage, document this and consider changing model family.
Do not assert linear/exponential from one or two intervals alone.
Agreed
Modelling | motion data, changing intervals
Student's time-position data or interval calculation suggests changing speed
Are equal-time changes in position becoming larger, smaller or irregular?
Timing/distance resolution may dominate short intervals; refer to earlier C24 record.
How does this support/challenge constant-speed prediction and subsequent modelling aim?
Consider appropriate rates of change, or form a position/time model from suitable evidence.
If a result is physically surprising, verify units and timing conventions, then explore a legitimate alternative.
Do not compute acceleration to unsupported precision.
Agreed
Modelling | labelled geometry and constraints
Student has drawn a useful scale/sketch or calculated an initial area/volume relation
What quantity is fixed, what varies and how are they related?
Confirm input dimensions/units; revisit precision only if newly relevant.
Why does the relationship help find an actionable optimum or geometric conclusion?
Derive the objective expression with the constraint; explore optimisation only once it begins.
If the geometry contradicts an assumed constraint, revise model setup rather than continuing algebra unchanged.
No stationary-point warnings until actually optimising.
Agreed
Modelling | calculated optimum is outside constraints
Student has ACTUALLY differentiated/compared candidates and result lies outside allowable domain
What value did the mathematics return, and why is it infeasible in context?
Check constraints, units and input sensitivity if these could change feasible choice.
Can the intended practical decision be answered by endpoints or realistic discrete options?
Evaluate feasible boundaries and compare admissible candidates; explain why this follows.
Acknowledge that the mathematical stationary point isn't a valid practical optimum; update claim rather than hide it.
Only suggest AFTER optimisation has actually been done (C40/C50), not after first sketch.
Agreed
Modelling | measured dimensional result
Student computes area, volume, speed or similar from measured input values
What derived value and units does this calculation produce?
If inherited input uncertainty was not already discussed, consider effect on reported digits/relative size of result.
Would the result meet the original design/decision aim within defensible accuracy?
Investigate sensitivity or the next relationship only where consequential.
If a numerical value is surprising, recheck units/formula and whether real geometry follows ideal assumptions.
Do not fabricate uncertainties or repeat elementary substitution at length.
Agreed
Modelling | fitted model misses actual observations
Student has ACTUALLY fitted a model and observed mismatched residuals/points
Where and how does the model deviate? Is a consistent pattern apparent?
Refer to measurement/source precision only if deviations are comparable to uncertainty.
Does the model still answer the aim accurately within a restricted domain?
Inspect meaningful residual pattern/sensitivity, justify an alternative model or restrict range.
Rather than accept poor fit and move on, ask which assumption or model form might explain it.
Fit criticism belongs to C40/C50 when a model was actually fitted.
Agreed
Modelling | fitted model unexpectedly strong
Student has ACTUALLY fitted a model and observed unusually good agreement
What supports the apparent agreement and over which input range?
Check whether precision/rounding or repeated use of calibration data overstates certainty.
Would the model's supported range cover the decision needed by beneficiary?
If prediction beyond fitted data is intended, consider independent observations where feasible.
Unexpectedly strong fit is not automatically suspicious; check whether it generalises before claiming certainty.
A high fit measure is not proof of a correct mechanism.
Agreed
Modelling | spatial points suggest nearest-location regions
Student has a labelled location sketch or coordinates
Which locations seem to compete to be nearest for the decision area?
Check map distances/scales and actual coordinate conventions.
Would a nearest-place partition support the original service/location advice?
Consider a course-appropriate Voronoi or distance calculation when relevant.
If visual closeness contradicts practical choice, reconsider whether straight-line distance measures what beneficiary needs.
No automatic assumption that travel time equals straight-line distance.
Agreed
Theory | first examples support conjecture
Student checked a small number of exact cases that appear to agree
What common structure actually appears across these examples?
Confirm calculations and scope of integer/domain examples, where relevant.
What GENERAL statement would advance the investigation beyond individual examples?
Formulate a precise conjecture and pursue proof or meaningful counterexample checks.
If a later case fails, preserve the failed conjecture and refine its conditions.
Multiple examples alone are not a proof.
Agreed
Theory | counterexample contradicts conjecture
Student ACTUALLY finds counterexample or special case that invalidates proposed universal claim
Which specific condition/example fails, and where did the original reasoning stop applying?
Verify logic and definitions, not measurement accuracy.
How might a narrower conjecture still address the aim or inspire new mathematics?
Identify valid conditions; seek a corrected claim or different proof route.
Explain why the surprise is mathematically important before revising the investigation.
Don't discard the example or invent an argument that 'nearly proves' the old conjecture.
Agreed
Any | initial calculation gives surprising value
Student explicitly reports numerical result conflicts with prediction/context
Is the value larger, smaller, opposite sign or unexpectedly impossible?
Check unit conversions and input rounding only if newly relevant; do not ask again if already checked.
Does the result change the intended decision or indicate original aim needs narrowing?
Verify essential setup; then test a different legitimate case or a sensitivity/constraint check.
Separate 'I may have made an error' from 'The model/expectation was wrong' and test rather than assume.
Don't use repeated elementary arithmetic as a substitute for interpretation.
Agreed
Statistics | visible clusters in combined scatter
Student notices group-specific clusters in actual paired data
Are clusters associated with known categories, conditions or time periods?
Sample counts within clusters and measurement variation may limit group comparisons.
Would separate interpretations be more relevant to the chosen beneficiary than a single overall association?
Compare groups appropriately, perhaps graph them SIDE BY SIDE on matching scales if the comparison genuinely helps.
If combined trend differs from expectations, examine justified subgroup patterns instead of suppressing a cluster.
No invented categories or multiple redundant scatter diagrams; avoid causal claims.
Agreed
Any | apparent effect may be comparable to measurement uncertainty
Student observes a small difference/change near actual measurement/source resolution
Is the apparent effect meaningfully distinguishable at the precision supported by data?
If C24 already gave sufficient justification, simply reference it; if not, revisit the specific precision issue.
Can the original aim be answered with a useful range or cautious conclusion instead?
Consider an appropriate uncertainty/sensitivity comparison only when mathematically justified.
A surprising tiny change may not support a strong directional claim; seek evidence or limit inference.
No spurious decimal places; no invented instrument errors.
Agreed
Any | little useful pattern or evidence
Student cannot yet identify a pattern, or original diagram adds nothing to story
Does the figure answer any part of the aim? Is absence of pattern itself informative?
Use confirmed evidence scope; avoid a checklist of generic limitations.
Is the original question still meaningful, or should it be narrowed honestly?
Explain no clear conclusion so far, plan one genuinely useful alternate view/check or move to a substantive question.
Don't 'fish' through endless diagrams until the prediction seems true; it's okay to remove a useless chart.
Not observing the expected effect can be a genuine finding.
Agreed
Any | calculation or diagram confirms an earlier conclusion
Student revisits an earlier result with no new information
What, if anything, is learned that the first figure/result did not show?
Reuse the previously justified accuracy; no repeated boilerplate.
Does repetition advance the aim or just restate earlier work?
Reference the existing figure/result and proceed to the next new mathematical question.
If a deliberate side-by-side comparison reveals a meaningful difference, state why, otherwise omit repetition.
No duplicate figures or lengthy repetitive calculations.
Agreed

Conditional brief note or 'Covered earlier' with reference to C24/C23.

Don't repeat limitations after every chart; if nothing new, refer to earlier discussion.
Agreed
Always

One short aim-linked statement.
Current aim and intended user; avoid rewriting aim automatically.
Observation can be inconclusive; do not promise advice.
Agreed
If prediction exists
How does the evidence relate to what you originally predicted, and WHY you predicted it?
Supports / challenges / unclear + short explanation.
Original dated prediction/WHY and anticipated meaning for beneficiary.

Optional contextual note.
benefitType, beneficiary, intendedUse and actual evidence

Only when student marks result as unexpected/unclear
Exactly what was different from your expectation? What could explain that, and which one check would genuinely distinguish the explanations?
Short discrepancy + optional on-demand suggestions; no mandatory explanation claim.
Student-confirmed observation and prediction (not automatic visual diagnosis).
Do not force progress until the discrepancy is considered; still allow Save/Not sure.
Agreed
After reflection (all paths)
What mathematical question follows from THIS observation, and WHY would the next method help answer it?
Student selects or writes next step; 1–3 optional suggestions.
Confirmed observed feature + route + actual data + course; plan.initialMaths only as context.
Do not automatically run PMCC from a scatter plot or offer PMCC limitations before use.
Agreed
When surprise involves data quality/measurement
What do your existing collection notes already tell you? Is there a specific data/source error or resolution issue to verify?
Optional check / return to C20 or C24.
C23/C24 records and relevant real data.
Do not invent errors or ask generic practical difficulties.
Agreed
When surprise involves a model/theoretical assumption
Which assumption, range or special case would be meaningful to vary or test?
Optional compare small case, model alternative or condition; only if appropriate.
Current model/conjecture, actual result; no new unsupported syllabus content.
Do not mistake an unexpected result for proof of model failure.
Agreed
When a planned method conflicts with actual pattern
Is the originally proposed method still sensible? If not, which course-appropriate method better addresses the observed question?
Keep / Revise / Not sure; student reason.
Initial maths selections, current observed pattern and aim.
A changed plan is positive reflection, not an automatic failure. No overfitting or fishing.
Agreed

Test ID
Given student context
What should happen
What must NOT happen
Expected meaningful outcome
Status
Scatter appears roughly linear; PMCC planned
C34 observation and C34B purpose first; C35H may suggest PMCC to QUANTIFY linear association if in course.
Don't run PMCC automatically or show PMCC-specific limitation before C40.
Student explains how PMCC addresses aim and why evidence motivates it.
To test
Predicted linear; actual scatter visibly curves
C34U asks exactly what differs and offers alternative shape/range checks.
Don't force PMCC because it was selected in Planning.
Preserve initial prediction, investigate curvature and choose next maths deliberately.
To test
Expected normal; actual histogram skewed
Student describes skew, revisits normal prediction; suggests appropriate summary/comparison.
Don't label curve normal or force normal probability model.
Explain effect on intended aim and next mathematics.
To test
Observed no clear correlation
Allow a worthwhile inconclusive observation; options to check range, sample, true absence.
No repeated chart fishing until a correlation appears.
Justified next check OR cautious conclusion; no forced positive result.
To test
Plot shows surprising outlier
Student may verify source and retain genuine value; discuss relevance to aim.
Do not delete automatically or pop PMCC limitations before PMCC is used.
Explain what is observed vs untested cause.
To test
Graph accuracy already analysed in C24
No repeat; simply refer to earlier accuracy record if sufficient.
No unnecessary mandatory 'accuracy discussion' box.
Avoid repeated boilerplate and preserve focus on meaningful reflection.
To test
New result small relative to source precision
Ask specific accuracy/uncertainty question, link to C24 where needed.
No invention of a tolerance or spurious decimal precision.
Determine whether stronger conclusion is defensible.
To test
Theoretical counterexample
Record contradicted conjecture and prompt narrower condition/proof.
No data collection or sampling prompts; don't hide the counterexample.
Unexpected result becomes mathematical direction.
To test
Optimisation result infeasible AFTER differentiation
Check admissible domain/endpoints and revise interpretation.
No stationary-point limitation while only drawing original sketch.
Method-stage limitation occurs only during current optimisation.
To test
Student changes beneficiary or aim
Offer review of current interpretation; preserve old prediction and observation.
No silent rewriting, deleting or presenting old impact as proved.
Student can return to stage without losing work.
To test
Student selects 'Not sure' after an unexpected finding
Preserve unresolved discrepancy, allow save and contextual examples later.
No gate demanding a fabricated cause.
Resume at same question, original data preserved.
To test
Student opts out of examples
Brief core questions remain; no 'show more' block.
No unwanted hint cards or automatically authored paragraph.
Student still provides what they see, aim and next action.
To test
Save/Resume: store the student's actual observation, accuracy-status, aim and prediction response, unexpected-result note, investigation/check and next-step rationale—not the example text.
